findings.title: The escaping requirement is not covered for every session-file field that is rendered
findings.why: A session containing a malicious reviewer/model/status/message field such as `` can still reach the generated panel HTML if only the vendor span is escaped; the single test for a vendor name does not establish the stated guarantee that nothing from a session file is unescaped.
findings.fix: Inventory every session-derived value used by panelView, escape each at the final HTML boundary (or render through one escaping helper), and add field-specific tests for every rendered text field, not just vendor names.
findings.verdict: It names a real, specific risk (session-file text reaching webview HTML through fields other than the one tested) and asks for the proportionate fix this family's own rules require: enumerate the sites and route them through one escaping helper rather than trusting a single-field test as proof of a blanket guarantee.

findings.title: The auto-open ownership design does not define how user opens are distinguished from panel opens
findings.why: The proposed second set only says that a person's toggle removes a key, but it does not specify the event/state transition that records a person opening a card. If a person opens a running round through the existing reveal path, the set can remain absent and the finish transition can close it, violating the promise that a person-opened round stays open; conversely, treating any reveal as panel-owned can close a manually reopened card.
findings.fix: Specify and test explicit transition handlers: panel auto-open adds ownership, user open clears ownership and marks the card user-owned, user close clears panel ownership, and finish only collapses entries still owned by the panel.
findings.verdict: It names a real gap in a state design: with a shared reveal path, the plan never says whether ownership is recorded at the auto-open trigger or inside reveal, and the two placements give opposite behaviour for a person-opened card at finish, so specifying and testing the transitions is a proportionate ask even though the first of its two scenarios is muddled.

findings.title: The plan does not define behavior for polling races and panel reloads around completion
findings.why: If a round is running in one refresh and finished in the next while a user toggle or extension-host/view reload occurs between those operations, the ownership set and expanded state can be updated in different orders; the finished card may remain expanded or a user-opened card may be collapsed. The tests cover a simple transition but not the failure-prone interleavings the feature depends on.
findings.fix: Define the state update as an atomic/idempotent refresh transition keyed by round identity, and add tests for finish-versus-toggle and finish-versus-view recreation, including killed/restarted panel state.
findings.verdict: It speculates about interleavings that a single-threaded webview processes in order, names no concrete defect in the plan, and asks for atomic transitions plus a battery of race tests for a risk whose worst case is a card left in the wrong expanded state, one click from fixed.

findings.title: The colour plan leaves collisions and palette evolution unspecified
findings.why: A deterministic index into a finite palette gives the same colour after restart, but two vendors whose hashes map to the same slot render identically, and changing the palette order or length in a later release changes existing vendors' colours. The only test uses two common names and therefore does not verify the broader stability promise.
findings.fix: Document collision as an accepted property or define a stable collision strategy, and test a collision pair plus palette changes; if cross-version stability is required, use a versioned palette and stable mapping contract.
findings.verdict: Hashing a handful of vendors into a small palette collides more often than not, and two vendors sharing a colour defeats the colour's only purpose, so naming the collision case is worth a sentence in the plan even though the versioned-palette half of the fix is more machinery than the risk warrants.

findings.title: Constraints: Single reviewer row renderer injects HTML spans into plain-text test consumers.
findings.why: The plan requires a single renderer for reviewer rows ('One renderer for a reviewer row, not a text one and an HTML one that drift. The text version is what the tests read today.') while step 5 introduces `<span class="vendor" style="...">` wrapping. Existing tests asserting on plain-text format (e.g., 'codex/PlanCritique — running') will receive raw HTML markup and fail.
findings.fix: Separate the raw text row model from the HTML markup decorator, or sanitize/strip tags in the shared renderer when evaluated in plain-text test contexts.

findings.title: Build order (panelProvider/panelView): Card expansion state changes trigger full panel telemetry probes.
findings.why: When a card transitions between open and closed, invoking the general panel view rebuild causes the panel to re-stat binaries, probe vendor CLIs, fetch GitHub release data, and download pricing tables, causing multi-second freezes on simple click or auto-collapse events.
findings.fix: Decouple expansion state handling and DOM toggle rendering from the heavy panel background data fetch and vendor probe lifecycle.

findings.title: Build order (rounds.ts): Placing theme color resolution in session parser creates an inverted dependency.
findings.why: Placing `vendorColour(name)` in `rounds.ts` ties session log parsing to UI theme palette concerns (`--vscode-charts-*`), forcing external UI consumers like spending tables to import the session parser.
findings.fix: Define `vendorColour` in an independent UI view utility module (e.g., `vendorColour.ts`) consumed by both round cards and spending rows.

findings.title: Ambiguous ownership logic causes data loss on restart
findings.why: The plan relies on the assumption that a round 'opened by the panel' can be identified solely by its presence in a specific set or its current state. If the extension host restarts or the round object is re-hydrated from a session file, the code loses the context of 'who opened it' because no persistent ID links the 'opened by panel' set to the round's history. Result: A round opened by the panel, finished, and then the extension restarts is treated as 'person opened' (because it's not in the pruned set) and stays open forever, or conversely, a person's round is auto-closed because it matches a stale state.
findings.fix: Add a deterministic ID field to the round object (e.g., `session_id` or `round_id`) and use it to match the 'opened by panel' state against the round's lifecycle events, rather than relying on object identity or timestamp proximity.
findings.verdict: The risk it names is real and matches the family's durable-status rule: an in-memory 'opened by the panel' set dies with the extension host, so a restart mislabels who owns a round and the auto-close logic goes wrong in one direction or the other, which the plan must answer with persisted state even though the proposed fix (adding an ID) is aimed at identity rather than at the persistence gap that actually causes it.

findings.title: Fable gating logic is fundamentally misaligned with system architecture
findings.why: The plan assumes `PanelService.FableIsUsable()` checks if Fable is a 'reviewer' in the provider list. Since Fable is the 'calling AI' and not a configured reviewer, this check returns false on every real machine. Result: The 'Split with Fable' checkbox becomes inert; users toggle it expecting a split, but the system ignores it because it waits for a non-existent reviewer configuration, leading to silent failure where the intended workflow never triggers.
findings.fix: Replace the `FableAvailable` flag with a direct check of the `CommandContext` for the presence of the Fable model instance or a configuration key that explicitly enables the 'Split' mode, rather than checking a provider list that Fable is not part of.
findings.verdict: The finding rests on an unsupported premise that contradicts this product's design: a Claude model is a configured reviewer row on the claude CLI, so gating on the provider list is the expected check, and the proposed fix asks the gate to detect which model is calling it, which neither the MCP server nor the extension can do.

findings.title: Synchronous expensive I/O on UI render path causes 20s latency
findings.why: The plan states the toggle must 'repaint to build a card's body', triggering a sequence of synchronous operations: reading config, stat-ing binary, probing CLIs, and fetching GitHub price tables. Result: When a user toggles the switch or opens a card, the UI freezes for up to 20 seconds while these blocking calls complete, causing the user to think the extension has hung or crashed, leading to double-toggling or premature closure.
findings.fix: Cache the result of the configuration read, server stat, CLI probe, and price table fetches in memory or a local store, and only re-evaluate on explicit configuration changes or a defined interval, rather than on every toggle repaint.
findings.verdict: It manufactures the defect from the quoted phrase: a webview 'repaint' rebuilds HTML from state the extension already holds, extension-host I/O is asynchronous and cannot freeze VS Code's UI, and the '20 seconds' is invented, so the only surviving content is generic caching advice the plan's wording already implies.

findings.title: Dead rounds report incorrect duration due to missing completion state
findings.why: The plan admits that 'a dead round is never written a completion time', so the system measures duration from the start time. Result: If a round crashes or times out (e.g., after 10 minutes) but the process doesn't die, the system calculates duration as 'current time - start time'. A round that died 360 minutes ago will report '361m 40s' instead of '10m', misleading the user about the actual runtime and potentially causing the system to think a long-running process is still active when it is dead.
findings.fix: Introduce a 'last known state' timestamp or explicit 'completion' flag in the round object that is written immediately upon the round's logical finish, rather than inferring completion from the absence of activity or measuring duration from start time.
findings.verdict: A dead round rendered with a start-to-now duration is a real stuck-in-flight display that this family's durable-status rule forbids, and the plan's own admission that no completion time exists is exactly why the card needs a heartbeat stamp or an explicit absence marker; the fix is half-misdirected (a completion flag cannot be written by a round that died) but the risk it names is genuine.

findings.title: Visual regression causes vendor names to appear struck-through
findings.why: The plan notes that the span class `who` (or `vendor`) inherits a border, radius, and padding from the `.vendor` class used for the settings card. Result: When a single word is rendered inside this container with tight line spacing, the border/padding creates a visual artifact that looks like a strikethrough line through the text. Users perceive the vendor name as 'deleted' or 'invalid', causing confusion about whether the split actually occurred.
findings.fix: Add a specific CSS class for the 'vendor' text span that overrides the default line-height and padding, or explicitly set `display: inline-block` with `line-height: normal` to prevent the text from being visually struck through by the container's border.
findings.verdict: A border, radius and padding inherited by an inline span render as a box around the text, not as a line through it, so the strikethrough artifact is invented and the fix addresses a defect that does not exist.

findings.title: Legacy rounds render as empty placeholders with misleading interaction cues
findings.why: The plan states that rounds recorded before per-reviewer detail became 'disclosures that opened into an apology'. Result: When a user clicks on a legacy round, they see a 'hand cursor' promising detail, but the content is empty or just an apology. This creates a false expectation of data, leading to user frustration when they realize the round has no actionable history, and the 'flat line' rendering makes it indistinguishable from a failed load.
findings.fix: Implement a fallback UI state for rounds recorded before per-reviewer detail existed, or explicitly mark them as 'legacy' with a distinct visual indicator, rather than rendering them as 'flat lines' with a hand cursor.
findings.verdict: It misreads the plan's own symptom description (legacy rounds as disclosures opening into an apology) as the proposed design, then asks for the distinct legacy state the plan already introduces, and the hand-cursor claim is asserted without any evidence.

If a user manually expanded a round on a branch or session that temporarily disappears (e.g. branch switch in git, session purge, or workspace filter update), their explicit toggle state is permanently discarded rather than preserved if the branch/session is returned to, reverting user manual state upon reload/re-render.

findings.title: Synchronous Thread.Sleep in retry loop blocks MCP server async request execution threads
findings.why: MoveOverExisting uses synchronous Thread.Sleep(20 * attempt) on IOException/UnauthorizedAccessException (up to 300ms total blocking sleep across 5 attempts). When multiple concurrent MCP requests or background saves hit contention on Windows file handles, worker threads on the thread pool or stdio handler are synchronously blocked.
findings.fix: Make MoveOverExisting async with await Task.Delay(20 * attempt, cancellationToken) if called from async paths, or keep retry backoff minimal without synchronous thread blocking.
findings.verdict: The sleep is bounded (at most 200 ms, not 300, since the last attempt does not sleep), happens only on a rare Windows contention path inside an already fully synchronous store whose file reads and writes block the same threads, and in a server whose rounds take minutes per reviewer, so converting the store to async is machinery out of proportion to a negligible, deliberate, well-commented trade.

findings.title: Vendor palette fallback color lacks explicit contrast guarantee for unknown vendors on non-standard themes
findings.why: For custom/unanchored vendors, vendorColour uses FNV-1a modulo over the 6 chart colors (--vscode-charts-*). If a custom vendor string hashes to a chart color that has low contrast in certain edge themes (or if the theme defines pale chart colors), the inline style color overrides the row text color entirely without a fallback class.
findings.fix: Add a CSS class alongside the inline style so theme-specific CSS rules can override chart variable contrast if needed.
findings.verdict: The palette is already the theme's own chart colours, defined by each theme to be legible on its background, so the contrast risk is speculative; it applies equally to the anchored vendors the finding exempts, and the proposed extra CSS-class hook is machinery out of proportion to a hypothetical pale theme.

findings.title: Retry loop in MoveOverExisting may hang indefinitely on persistent file locks
findings.why: The `MoveOverExisting` method retries 5 times with a sleep of `20 * attempt` milliseconds. If a file lock (e.g., from an antivirus scanner or a slow indexer) persists longer than the total retry window (approx 150ms), the method throws. However, if the lock is transient but the system is under heavy load, the retry logic might not be sufficient, or worse, if the `Thread.Sleep` is interrupted or the process is killed during the sleep, the temporary file might be left behind if the `finally` block logic is not robust. More critically, if the `File.Move` throws a different exception (e.g., `PathTooLongException`) that isn't caught by the `catch` block, the loop exits early, potentially leaving the temp file orphaned if the `TryDelete` isn't called. The specific risk is a race condition where the file is held by a scanner; the retry might succeed, but if it fails after 5 attempts, the exception is thrown, but the `finally` block ensures cleanup. The real risk is if the `MoveOverExisting` is called in a tight loop without sufficient delay, or if the OS file system state is inconsistent. The finding is that the retry logic is hardcoded and might not cover all edge cases of file locking on Windows, leading to silent failures if the exception handling is too broad or too narrow.
findings.fix: Ensure the retry loop in MoveOverExisting uses a bounded, non-exponential backoff or a maximum total duration to prevent indefinite hanging during transient file system locks, and verify that the final exception is logged with full context before re-throwing.
findings.verdict: The central claim is false: the loop is bounded to five attempts and about 200 ms of sleep, the `finally` in `Save` deletes the scratch file on every exit path including uncaught exception types, and the finding contradicts itself mid-paragraph before asking for a bound that already exists.

findings.title: Vendor name color interpolation may allow style injection if not sanitized
findings.why: The code `style="color:${vendorColour(r.provider)}"` interpolates the result of `vendorColour` directly into the HTML. While `vendorColour` returns a CSS variable string (e.g., `var(--vscode-charts-blue)`), if the function were to return a raw hex value or if the input `r.provider` contained a malicious string that bypassed the `trim().toLowerCase()` logic (e.g., via a Unicode trick or a specific character encoding), it could inject a style property. The current implementation uses `escapeHtml` for the text content, but the style attribute is constructed from a function that relies on the input. If `vendorColour` were to return something like `url('javascript:alert(1)')` (though unlikely given the palette), it could be exploited. The specific risk is if `vendorColour` is modified in the future to return a hex value or if the input `r.provider` is not strictly controlled, leading to a style injection vulnerability where an attacker could override the color or inject CSS properties.
findings.fix: Ensure `vendorColour` is called with a sanitized string before being interpolated into the `style` attribute, or use a CSS variable that is pre-validated, to prevent potential style injection if the vendor name contains unexpected characters.

findings.title: Potential race condition in `nextOpenRounds` if `roundKey` is not unique
findings.why: The `nextOpenRounds` function uses `roundKey` to identify rounds. If two rounds have the same key (e.g., same stage, number, and branch), the `Set` will treat them as the same entity. This could lead to one round's state (open/closed) overwriting the other's, causing a UI inconsistency where one round is closed while the other is open, or vice versa. The risk is low if `roundKey` is guaranteed to be unique, but if the logic for generating `roundKey` changes or if there's a bug in the data source, this could cause silent state corruption.
findings.fix: Add a check to ensure that `roundKey` is unique across all rounds before adding to the `open` set, or handle collisions by appending a suffix or using a composite key.
findings.verdict: It is speculative about a hypothetical future bug in roundKey rather than anything this code does, mislabels a key collision as a race condition, and the proposed uniqueness check is machinery out of proportion to a risk that would break the whole rounds list anyway, not just this policy.

findings.title: Race condition in session file cleanup due to exception handling order
findings.why: In `SessionStore.Save`, the `finally` block calls `TryDelete(temp)` unconditionally after `MoveOverExisting`. If `MoveOverExisting` throws an exception on its final attempt (line 175), the `finally` block executes. However, if the file move succeeds but the `TryDelete` fails (e.g., due to a race with another process that just acquired the file), the exception is swallowed. More critically, if `MoveOverExisting` throws *before* the loop completes (e.g., on the first attempt), the `finally` block runs, but the file might still be in a transient state. The current structure risks leaving `.tmp` files behind if the move fails after the loop, or deleting a file that another process is still using if the timing is tight. The `TryDelete` should be more robustly tied to the success of the move.
findings.fix: Move the `TryDelete(temp)` call inside the `try` block of `MoveOverExisting` or ensure it runs after the retry loop completes, rather than unconditionally after the loop. Currently, if `MoveOverExisting` throws on the final attempt, the `finally` block executes, but if the exception happens inside the loop before the final throw, the cleanup logic might be inconsistent or the `finally` block might run before the file is fully moved in edge cases.
findings.verdict: The finding misreads the code: the scratch name is unique per process and write so no other writer can hold it, File.Move is atomic so there is no transient state, File.Delete on an already-moved temp is a silent no-op, and the finally already runs after the retry loop completes, so none of the described races exist and the proposed fix restates the current structure.

findings.title: Potential mutation of input Set in `nextOpenRounds`
findings.why: In `nextOpenRounds`, the code creates `const panelOpened = new Set(previous.panelOpened);` (line 52). Later, it calls `panelOpened.delete(key)` (line 63). While this creates a new Set, if `previous.panelOpened` is a reference to a Set that is used elsewhere, and the code were to mutate the original `previous.panelOpened` directly (which it doesn't here, but the pattern is risky), it could cause issues. More importantly, the logic `const panelOpened = new Set(previous.panelOpened);` creates a shallow copy. If `previous.panelOpened` contains objects (it contains strings, so this is fine), it's safe. However, the line `const open = new Set(previous.open);` (line 51) and `const autoOpened = new Set(previous.autoOpened);` (line 50) are also shallow copies. The main risk is if `previous` is mutated elsewhere while this function runs, but the bigger issue is the logic: `panelOpened.delete(key)` modifies the local `panelOpened` Set. If `previous.panelOpened` is a reference to a Set that is used by the caller, and the caller expects it to be immutable, this could be a problem. But since it's a new Set, it's mostly fine. The real issue is that `open`, `autoOpened`, and `panelOpened` are all created as new Sets, but then `open.add(key)` (line 56) and `autoOpened.add(key)` (line 57) modify them. The return statement creates new arrays from these Sets. This is generally safe, but the logic `const panelOpened = new Set(previous.panelOpened);` followed by `panelOpened.delete(key)` is correct. The finding is minor because the code is mostly correct, but the pattern of creating new Sets and then modifying them could be clearer.
findings.fix: Add a check to ensure `panelOpened` is not mutated directly in `nextOpenRounds` before filtering, or use a new Set for the result to avoid potential mutation side effects if the input array is reused.
findings.verdict: The finding concedes repeatedly that the code is correct, cites line numbers that do not match the file, and describes no real defect: the function copies the readonly input arrays into fresh local Sets, mutates only those, and returns new arrays, so there is no input mutation to guard against.

findings.title: Unnecessary recalculation of open rounds state on every tick
findings.why: In `panelProvider.ts`, the `expanded` method calls `nextOpenRounds(this.rounds, cards)` on every tick (line 165). If the `cards` array (derived from `sessions`) hasn't changed, this recalculates the entire state machine. While the logic is fast, doing this on every 5-second tick for a large number of rounds could be optimized by checking if `cards` has changed (e.g., by comparing lengths or hashes) before calling `nextOpenRounds`. This is a minor performance issue but could become significant if the number of rounds grows large.
findings.fix: Cache the result of `nextOpenRounds` if the input `cards` hasn't changed, or debounce the call to avoid unnecessary recalculations on every tick.
findings.verdict: The state machine runs over a handful of round cards every five seconds beside file reads, CLI probes and price fetches that dwarf it, and the finding itself only speculates about a large-list case that this panel never has, so the cache or debounce it asks for is machinery out of proportion to any risk.

findings.title: Retry loop in MoveOverExisting may hang indefinitely on persistent file locks
findings.why: The `MoveOverExisting` method retries 5 times with a sleep of `20 * attempt` milliseconds. If a file lock (e.g., from an antivirus scanner or a slow indexer) persists longer than the total retry window (approx 150ms), the method throws. However, if the lock is transient but the system is under heavy load, the retry logic might not be sufficient, or worse, if the `Thread.Sleep` is interrupted or the process is killed during the sleep, the temporary file might be left behind if the `finally` block logic is not robust. More critically, if the `File.Move` throws a different exception (e.g., `PathTooLongException`) that isn't caught by the `catch` block, the loop exits early, potentially leaving the temp file orphaned if the `TryDelete` isn't called. The specific risk is a race condition where the file is held by a scanner; the retry might succeed, but if it fails after 5 attempts, the exception is thrown, but the `finally` block ensures cleanup. The real risk is if the `MoveOverExisting` is called in a tight loop without sufficient delay, or if the OS file system state is inconsistent. The finding is that the retry logic is hardcoded and might not cover all edge cases of file locking on Windows, leading to silent failures if the exception handling is too broad or too narrow.
findings.fix: Ensure the retry loop in MoveOverExisting uses a bounded, non-exponential backoff or a maximum total duration to prevent indefinite hanging during transient file system locks, and verify that the final exception is logged with full context before re-throwing.
findings.verdict: The finding is wrong about this code: the loop is bounded to five attempts with linear sleeps totalling about 200 ms and the last attempt rethrows, the temp file is deleted in Save's finally on every exception type, and the finding contradicts itself mid-paragraph, so it names no defect a careful engineer would change.

findings.title: Vendor name color interpolation may allow style injection if not sanitized
findings.why: The code `style="color:${vendorColour(r.provider)}"` interpolates the result of `vendorColour` directly into the HTML. While `vendorColour` returns a CSS variable string (e.g., `var(--vscode-charts-blue)`), if the function were to return a raw hex value or if the input `r.provider` contained a malicious string that bypassed the `trim().toLowerCase()` logic (e.g., via a Unicode trick or a specific character encoding), it could inject a style property. The current implementation uses `escapeHtml` for the text content, but the style attribute is constructed from a function that relies on the input. If `vendorColour` were to return something like `url('javascript:alert(1)')` (though unlikely given the palette), it could be exploited. The specific risk is if `vendorColour` is modified in the future to return a hex value or if the input `r.provider` is not strictly controlled, leading to a style injection vulnerability where an attacker could override the color or inject CSS properties.
findings.fix: Ensure `vendorColour` is called with a sanitized string before being interpolated into the `style` attribute, or use a CSS variable that is pre-validated, to prevent potential style injection if the vendor name contains unexpected characters.
findings.verdict: The finding concedes that vendorColour returns a fixed palette CSS variable and only injects if the function or its input were changed in the future, so it names no defect in this code and asks for sanitisation out of proportion to a risk that does not exist here.

findings.title: Potential race condition in `nextOpenRounds` if `roundKey` is not unique
findings.why: The `nextOpenRounds` function uses `roundKey` to identify rounds. If two rounds have the same key (e.g., same stage, number, and branch), the `Set` will treat them as the same entity. This could lead to one round's state (open/closed) overwriting the other's, causing a UI inconsistency where one round is closed while the other is open, or vice versa. The risk is low if `roundKey` is guaranteed to be unique, but if the logic for generating `roundKey` changes or if there's a bug in the data source, this could cause silent state corruption.
findings.fix: Add a check to ensure that `roundKey` is unique across all rounds before adding to the `open` set, or handle collisions by appending a suffix or using a composite key.
findings.verdict: It is speculation about a hypothetical bug in roundKey rather than anything this code does, mislabels a key collision as a race, and asks for uniqueness machinery out of proportion to a risk the finding itself admits is low.

findings.title: Race condition in session file cleanup due to exception handling order
findings.why: In `SessionStore.Save`, the `finally` block calls `TryDelete(temp)` unconditionally after `MoveOverExisting`. If `MoveOverExisting` throws an exception on its final attempt (line 175), the `finally` block executes. However, if the file move succeeds but the `TryDelete` fails (e.g., due to a race with another process that just acquired the file), the exception is swallowed. More critically, if `MoveOverExisting` throws *before* the loop completes (e.g., on the first attempt), the `finally` block runs, but the file might still be in a transient state. The current structure risks leaving `.tmp` files behind if the move fails after the loop, or deleting a file that another process is still using if the timing is tight. The `TryDelete` should be more robustly tied to the success of the move.
findings.fix: Move the `TryDelete(temp)` call inside the `try` block of `MoveOverExisting` or ensure it runs after the retry loop completes, rather than unconditionally after the loop. Currently, if `MoveOverExisting` throws on the final attempt, the `finally` block executes, but if the exception happens inside the loop before the final throw, the cleanup logic might be inconsistent or the `finally` block might run before the file is fully moved in edge cases.
findings.verdict: The scratch file is unique per write (pid + guid) and belongs to this writer alone, so the finally-delete is correct on every path: a no-op after a successful move and the right cleanup after a failed one, and no other process can be using it ΓÇö the finding misreads the structure and describes races the code cannot have.

findings.title: Potential mutation of input Set in `nextOpenRounds`
findings.why: In `nextOpenRounds`, the code creates `const panelOpened = new Set(previous.panelOpened);` (line 52). Later, it calls `panelOpened.delete(key)` (line 63). While this creates a new Set, if `previous.panelOpened` is a reference to a Set that is used elsewhere, and the code were to mutate the original `previous.panelOpened` directly (which it doesn't here, but the pattern is risky), it could cause issues. More importantly, the logic `const panelOpened = new Set(previous.panelOpened);` creates a shallow copy. If `previous.panelOpened` contains objects (it contains strings, so this is fine), it's safe. However, the line `const open = new Set(previous.open);` (line 51) and `const autoOpened = new Set(previous.autoOpened);` (line 50) are also shallow copies. The main risk is if `previous` is mutated elsewhere while this function runs, but the bigger issue is the logic: `panelOpened.delete(key)` modifies the local `panelOpened` Set. If `previous.panelOpened` is a reference to a Set that is used by the caller, and the caller expects it to be immutable, this could be a problem. But since it's a new Set, it's mostly fine. The real issue is that `open`, `autoOpened`, and `panelOpened` are all created as new Sets, but then `open.add(key)` (line 56) and `autoOpened.add(key)` (line 57) modify them. The return statement creates new arrays from these Sets. This is generally safe, but the logic `const panelOpened = new Set(previous.panelOpened);` followed by `panelOpened.delete(key)` is correct. The finding is minor because the code is mostly correct, but the pattern of creating new Sets and then modifying them could be clearer.
findings.fix: Add a check to ensure `panelOpened` is not mutated directly in `nextOpenRounds` before filtering, or use a new Set for the result to avoid potential mutation side effects if the input array is reused.
findings.verdict: The function already copies every input into a fresh Set and returns new arrays, so no input is mutated; the finding concedes this repeatedly, cites line numbers that do not match the file, and proposes a fix for a defect it never identifies.

findings.title: Unnecessary recalculation of open rounds state on every tick
findings.why: In `panelProvider.ts`, the `expanded` method calls `nextOpenRounds(this.rounds, cards)` on every tick (line 165). If the `cards` array (derived from `sessions`) hasn't changed, this recalculates the entire state machine. While the logic is fast, doing this on every 5-second tick for a large number of rounds could be optimized by checking if `cards` has changed (e.g., by comparing lengths or hashes) before calling `nextOpenRounds`. This is a minor performance issue but could become significant if the number of rounds grows large.
findings.fix: Cache the result of `nextOpenRounds` if the input `cards` hasn't changed, or debounce the call to avoid unnecessary recalculations on every tick.
findings.verdict: A pure O(n) pass over a handful of round cards every five seconds is negligible beside the file reads, version checks and HTTP probes the same render already performs, and the proposed change-detection would cost about as much as the recalculation it avoids while adding state to keep consistent.

findings.title: Atomic claim across processes relies on transient environment variables rather than persistent state.

findings.title: No mechanism exists to enforce the 'floor' for epics of epics without external state.

For example, if a user runs the plan on a branch that was already split once, but the 'caller' (the script invoking the plan) doesn't track that it was already split, the system will split the epic again, creating an infinite recursion of epics until memory or token limits are hit.

findings.title: Expired-claim replacement is not atomic across processes
findings.why: The requirement says, "The claim is atomic across processes: two servers sharing a data directory cannot both give it." Concurrent processes can both observe an expired file, race on `File.Delete`, and cause the loser to enter the fail-open handler and return `true` while the winner creates the new claim.
findings.fix: Use an atomic expiration-replacement protocol that distinguishes delete contention from an unwritable store, and never grant the order for a claim-file race.
findings.verdict: The ExistsΓåÆDeleteΓåÆCreateNew sequence on an expired stamp lets a second process delete the first process's freshly written claim (or hit a sharing-violation/pending-delete IOException with Exists false and fall into the fail-open branch), so both return true ΓÇö contradicting the code's own 'the only race there is' comment and the stated cross-process atomicity requirement; the reliability rule's 'fence the release' point applies directly.

findings.title: Deleting an expired claim is not atomic with creating its replacement
findings.why: Two processes can both read an expired stamp; process A pauses, process B deletes and creates a fresh claim, then A deletes B's fresh claim and creates its own. Both return true, so both callers issue the split order and the recursive split problem can recur.
findings.fix: Serialize the expired-claim replacement across processes, then re-read the stamp while holding the lock before deleting and creating the replacement.
findings.verdict: The delete-then-CreateNew sequence on the expired path is a real TOCTOU that lets a second process discard a fresh claim and both return true, directly contradicting the code's own comment that CreateNew is the only race; the window is narrow and the failure soft, but it breaks the exact atomicity this class was written to provide, so an engineer would want to fix it (a rename-away of the expired file would do, cheaper than the proposed cross-process lock).

findings.title: Unconditional File.Delete in TryClaimSplitOrder creates a race condition where concurrent callers delete each other's claims and both issue split orders
findings.why: When two processes execute TryClaimSplitOrder concurrently for an unclaimed caller, both evaluate StillRemembered as false. If Process A creates the claim file first and closes the stream, Process B reaches File.Exists / File.Delete, deletes Process A's newly written claim file, and then creates its own via FileMode.CreateNew. Both processes return true and issue duplicate split orders, defeating the cross-process atomicity guarantee.
findings.fix: Avoid deleting the file before creation; attempt atomic creation first with FileMode.CreateNew, and only attempt cleanup/replacement if the existing file is confirmed expired under a shared lock or atomic rename.
findings.verdict: The unconditional delete between the expiry check and CreateNew is a real TOCTOU that lets a second process erase a fresh claim and both return true, directly contradicting the code's own comment that CreateNew is the only race, and the fix (create first, delete only after re-confirming expiry) is small and proportionate.

findings.title: Unsynchronized File.Delete followed by FileMode.CreateNew creates a race window on expired claims
findings.why: When a claim expires, two concurrent processes checking `File.Exists(file)` both call `File.Delete(file)` followed by `new FileStream(file, FileMode.CreateNew...)`. If Process A creates the file between Process B's check and Process B's `File.Delete(file)`, Process B will delete Process A's freshly created claim file and then create its own claim. Both processes succeed in claiming the split order (`TryClaimSplitOrder` returns `true` for both), violating atomicity and issuing duplicate split orders to the caller.
findings.fix: Open the file with `FileMode.OpenOrCreate` with exclusive share (`FileShare.None`), read the timestamp from the locked stream, and update it in-place or recreate only within the held stream lock instead of deleting the file prior to `FileMode.CreateNew`.
findings.verdict: The unconditional File.Delete before CreateNew is an unfenced release: on an expired stamp a second server can delete the first's fresh claim and both return true, so the code's own promise of atomicity and the line-111 comment that CreateNew is the only race are false, and although the window is narrow and the failure soft, it is exactly the two-run-again defect the family's lock rule names and the suggested exclusive open-read-write fix is proportionate.

findings.title: Race condition in atomic claim due to pre-check deletion outside critical section
findings.why: The code checks `StillRemembered` (read), then deletes the file (write), then attempts `CreateNew` (write). If a second server deletes the file between the check and the delete, or if the delete fails silently, the `CreateNew` might succeed for the second server while the first server's logic assumed it was the only one. More critically, if `File.Delete` throws (e.g., file locked by another process), the code falls through to `CreateNew` which might succeed, but the state is inconsistent. The specific race: Server A checks `StillRemembered` (false), Server B checks `StillRemembered` (false). Server A deletes file. Server B deletes file (or tries to). Server A creates file. Server B creates file (fails with IOException). The `catch` block for `IOException` checks `File.Exists(file)`. If Server B's delete succeeded, `File.Exists` is true, so it returns false. If Server B's delete failed (file locked), `File.Exists` is true, returns false. But if Server A's delete failed, Server B creates, then Server A creates (fails). The logic relies on `File.Delete` being atomic or the `CreateNew` failing if the file exists. The real issue is the `File.Delete` is outside the `try` block that catches the `IOException` from `CreateNew`. If `File.Delete` throws, the code falls to the `catch (Exception e)` block, which returns `true` (success) even though the claim might not have been written. Wait, looking closer: `File.Delete` is outside the `try`. If it throws, it goes to `catch (Exception e)`. The `catch` block returns `true`. This means if the delete fails (e.g. permission denied on the file itself), the method returns `true` (claim succeeded) even though the file might not have been written. This is a silent failure where the claim is 'given' but not persisted.
findings.fix: Move the `File.Delete(file)` call inside the `try` block, immediately after the `StillRemembered` check, or wrap it in its own try-catch before the `CreateNew` attempt.
findings.verdict: The finding's central claim is false ΓÇö `File.Delete` is already inside the `try` (lines 108ΓÇô121), so its fix is a no-op ΓÇö and the `return true` on an unwritable claim is the documented, warned fail-open, not a silent failure; the one real hole in delete-then-CreateNew (a peer deleting a just-written fresh claim after its stream closes) is never actually named in the rambling scenario.

findings.title: Warning message for unwritable store lacks context for debugging
findings.why: When the store is unwritable, the code logs a warning: `the split-order memory at {Dir} could not be written`. If a user or operator sees this, they don't know *which* caller triggered it or *which* specific file failed. The message is generic. In a multi-caller environment, this makes debugging 'why is my split order failing?' difficult without checking logs for every caller.
findings.fix: Ensure the `warn` action is called with a specific, actionable message that includes the caller ID and the specific file path, not just a generic warning.
findings.verdict: The failure it worries about is a property of the directory (unwritable, full disk), not of any caller, so naming the caller adds nothing; the exception message already carries the path, and the finding's premise that a split order is 'failing' misreads the documented fail-open, where the warning itself says the order is still given.

findings.title: Potential redundant file system operations in high-concurrency scenarios
findings.why: The code calls `File.Exists(file)` and then `File.Delete(file)` and then `new FileStream(file, FileMode.CreateNew...)`. In a high-concurrency scenario with many servers, this involves multiple file system calls (stat, delete, create) for a single logical operation. While `CreateNew` is atomic, the pre-checks and deletions add overhead. If the file is frequently accessed, this could be optimized by using a single `FileStream` with `FileMode.OpenOrCreate` and a lock, or by relying solely on `CreateNew` and handling the exception if the file exists (which implies a race). The current approach is safe but potentially slower than necessary.
findings.fix: Cache the `FileFor` result or ensure `File.Exists` and `CreateNew` are not called on the same path twice in rapid succession without proper locking if high concurrency is expected.
findings.verdict: The claim runs once per review round (minutes of vendor CLI time) across a handful of servers on one machine, so three syscalls are noise, and the proposed fixes are either pointless (caching a SHA-256 of a short string) or wrong (a lock instead of the CreateNew the code already relies on and documents).

findings.title: Deleting an expired claim before CreateNew makes the claim non-atomic across processes
findings.why: The scope requires: “The claim is atomic across processes: two servers sharing a data directory cannot both give it.” Two processes can both observe an expired file; one can delete and recreate it, then the other can delete that fresh claim and successfully create its own, allowing duplicate orders.
findings.fix: Serialize expiry replacement with an exclusive lock, or use an atomic claim/renewal protocol that never deletes a file another process may have just created.
findings.verdict: The interleaving is real on this code: with an expired stamp, process A can delete-then-CreateNew and close its handle, after which process B's File.Exists/Delete removes A's fresh claim and B's CreateNew also succeeds, so both return true ΓÇö contradicting the scope's cross-process atomicity requirement and the line-111 comment claiming CreateNew is the only race, and it is fixable with a small change (atomic rename of the stale file, or an exclusive open-and-overwrite) rather than heavy machinery.

findings.title: The order predicate is evaluated twice instead of once for issuing and claiming
findings.why: The constraint says: “The condition that issues the order and the condition that claims it are ONE question asked once.” The code calls `OrdersSplit(provisional)` to decide whether to claim, then calls `OrdersSplit(context)` again to decide whether it issued the order.
findings.fix: Compute the split-order predicate once, use that result to conditionally claim, and derive logging/command handling from the same stored result.
findings.verdict: The two calls evaluate different inputs ΓÇö `provisional` before the claim and `context` after it ΓÇö so the second is not a repeat but the check that a denied claim does not log an order that was never issued; the constraint is met by using one predicate function, and the proposed single-evaluation fix would log 'split ordered' when the claim failed.

findings.title: Expired-claim replacement is not atomic across processes
findings.why: With an expired marker present, process A checks that it exists and pauses; process B deletes it and creates the new claim; A then deletes B's fresh claim and creates its own. Both calls return true, so two servers issue the split order despite the claimed atomic guarantee.
findings.fix: Serialize expiry replacement with a per-caller OS lock held across re-read, delete, and CreateNew, or use an atomic replacement protocol that never deletes a claim another process may have created.
findings.verdict: The interleaving is real (A's File.Exists/Delete can remove B's freshly created claim on an expired marker, so both CreateNew calls succeed) and it directly contradicts the code's own line-111 claim that CreateNew is 'the only race there is', which the reliability rule requires a lock's header to state honestly even if the chosen fix is just to record the residual.

findings.title: An I/O failure after claim-file creation is mistaken for a competing claim
findings.why: If CreateNew succeeds but writing the timestamp fails, for example because the disk fills, the file exists when the IOException is caught. The method returns false without warning, withholding the split order and silently failing closed; the same misclassification can occur for unrelated I/O errors while an old marker exists.
findings.fix: Treat only the specific CreateNew already-exists/share-violation error as a lost race; warn and return true for write or other I/O failures, cleaning up a partial marker when safe.
findings.verdict: The catch filter `when (File.Exists(file))` cannot distinguish a lost CreateNew race from a write/flush failure after CreateNew succeeded (or a failed Delete of a stale marker), so the very case the remarks promise fails OPEN ΓÇö a full disk ΓÇö instead returns false with no warning, silently withholding the order on every retry; narrowing the lost-race branch to the CreateNew call is a small, proportionate fix.

findings.title: TOCTOU deletion of valid claim files during concurrent calls allows duplicate split claims
findings.why: When two concurrent processes or threads call TryClaimSplitOrder for the same caller, both may find that File.Exists(file) is true (or one process expired/recreating). Process A executes File.Delete(file). If Process B had just written a valid active claim right after File.Delete or before it, Process A deletes Process B's brand new active claim file and proceeds to FileMode.CreateNew successfully. Both processes then return true, violating the atomic split order guarantee.
findings.fix: Catch IOException and check File.Exists(file) inside a retry loop, or open with FileMode.Open and check if the existing file is still valid/remembered rather than unconditionally deleting before CreateNew.
findings.verdict: The unconditional File.Delete between the stamp read and the CreateNew reintroduces exactly the read-then-write race the CreateNew was added to remove ΓÇö a peer that claimed in the gap has its fresh, valid stamp deleted and both callers return true ΓÇö so the comment 'the only race there is' is false, the release is unfenced in the way reliability.md's lock rule forbids, and a cheap fix (delete only the stamp you read, or move-then-create) exists.

findings.title: TryClaimSplitOrder consumes caller's split claim before checking if the round passes or produces commands
findings.why: TryClaimSplitOrder is called when constructing the CommandContext before the round verdict or final answer is fully determined. If GateCommands.OrdersSplit(provisional) is true based on settings/input, the file claim is permanently created on disk. If the plan round subsequently errors, fails validation, or crashes before returning the split order to the caller, the caller has permanently lost its split claim and subsequent retries will falsely treat it as already split (a piece), failing to ever split the plan.
findings.fix: Only execute TryClaimSplitOrder after verifying that the round actually passes and produces an answer with split commands, or compensate if the round fails/does not issue.
findings.verdict: The claim is already gated on the verdict (PlanStage requires MayProceed(completed.Verdict) and OrdersSplit checks it), so the finding's main premise is wrong; the only residual is a Save or audit throw between line 581 and the return, a rare I/O failure whose compensation machinery is out of proportion to a Minor risk.

However, the implementation returns `true` when the store is unwritable (fail-open), meaning the caller got the order despite the write failing. This contradicts the standard semantic of `Try` methods where `false` indicates failure.
findings.fix: Rename `TryClaimSplitOrder` to `RecordSplitOrder` or ensure the method name reflects the atomic claim nature in the public API if the name is intended to be descriptive of the action rather than the return value.

findings.title: The `warn` action is only invoked in the `catch (Exception e)` block, but not in the `catch (IOException) when (File.Exists(file))` block.

This creates an inconsistency where a race condition (someone else claiming) is silent, while a store failure (unwritable) is warned. The rule states 'a warning rather than silently disabling', implying warnings should be consistent for failures.
findings.fix: Ensure the `warn` action is invoked consistently for all failure cases or document that it is only invoked for specific exceptions.

findings.title: Variable name `provisional` is used for a `CommandContext` that is immediately used to create another `context` variable, which may cause confusion.

The naming convention in the project (e.g., `CallerSessions`, `PanelService`) suggests clear, descriptive names. Using `provisional` for a temporary state that is immediately used to create the final state is less clear than using a more descriptive name or reusing the variable.

findings.title: Race condition in atomic claim due to pre-check deletion outside critical section
findings.why: The code checks `StillRemembered` (read), then deletes the file (write), then attempts `CreateNew` (write). If a second server deletes the file between the check and the delete, or if the delete fails silently, the `CreateNew` might succeed for the second server while the first server's logic assumed it was the only one. More critically, if `File.Delete` throws (e.g., file locked by another process), the code falls through to `CreateNew` which might succeed, but the state is inconsistent. The specific race: Server A checks `StillRemembered` (false), Server B checks `StillRemembered` (false). Server A deletes file. Server B deletes file (or tries to). Server A creates file. Server B creates file (fails with IOException). The `catch` block for `IOException` checks `File.Exists(file)`. If Server B's delete succeeded, `File.Exists` is true, so it returns false. If Server B's delete failed (file locked), `File.Exists` is true, returns false. But if Server A's delete failed, Server B creates, then Server A creates (fails). The logic relies on `File.Delete` being atomic or the `CreateNew` failing if the file exists. The real issue is the `File.Delete` is outside the `try` block that catches the `IOException` from `CreateNew`. If `File.Delete` throws, the code falls to the `catch (Exception e)` block, which returns `true` (success) even though the claim might not have been written. Wait, looking closer: `File.Delete` is outside the `try`. If it throws, it goes to `catch (Exception e)`. The `catch` block returns `true`. This means if the delete fails (e.g. permission denied on the file itself), the method returns `true` (claim succeeded) even though the file might not have been written. This is a silent failure where the claim is 'given' but not persisted.
findings.fix: Move the `File.Delete(file)` call inside the `try` block, immediately after the `StillRemembered` check, or wrap it in its own try-catch before the `CreateNew` attempt.
findings.verdict: Its central claim is false ΓÇö File.Delete is already inside the try block, so the proposed fix is a no-op ΓÇö and its walked-through interleavings all end correctly while missing the one real hazard (a peer's unconditional delete removing a freshly written claim), leaving nothing an engineer can act on.

findings.title: Warning message for unwritable store lacks context for debugging
findings.why: When the store is unwritable, the code logs a warning: `the split-order memory at {Dir} could not be written`. If a user or operator sees this, they don't know *which* caller triggered it or *which* specific file failed. The message is generic. In a multi-caller environment, this makes debugging 'why is my split order failing?' difficult without checking logs for every caller.
findings.fix: Ensure the `warn` action is called with a specific, actionable message that includes the caller ID and the specific file path, not just a generic warning.
findings.verdict: The warning already names the directory and carries the exception's own message (which for IOException/UnauthorizedAccessException usually includes the failing path), the failure is environmental rather than per-caller so a caller id would not help diagnose it, and the finding misreads the consequence ΓÇö the order is given, not withheld, so nothing is 'failing' for the caller.

findings.title: Potential redundant file system operations in high-concurrency scenarios
findings.why: The code calls `File.Exists(file)` and then `File.Delete(file)` and then `new FileStream(file, FileMode.CreateNew...)`. In a high-concurrency scenario with many servers, this involves multiple file system calls (stat, delete, create) for a single logical operation. While `CreateNew` is atomic, the pre-checks and deletions add overhead. If the file is frequently accessed, this could be optimized by using a single `FileStream` with `FileMode.OpenOrCreate` and a lock, or by relying solely on `CreateNew` and handling the exception if the file exists (which implies a race). The current approach is safe but potentially slower than necessary.
findings.fix: Cache the `FileFor` result or ensure `File.Exists` and `CreateNew` are not called on the same path twice in rapid succession without proper locking if high concurrency is expected.
findings.verdict: This path runs at most once per caller per day and the Exists/Delete pre-step is what clears an expired stamp so CreateNew can succeed, so the three syscalls are neither a measurable cost nor redundant, and the proposed OpenOrCreate-plus-lock alternative would discard the very atomicity the code was built around.
